Photograph: Heiko Becker/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Would-be parcel bomber convicted in German court Russian-led plot was exposed when participants sent trial packages carrying GPS trackers through Ukrainian and German post. What we know on day 1,638 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Tue 18 Aug 2026 21.37 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 00.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A German court has convicted a Ukrainian man over a plot to send parcel bombs in Europe at the behest of Russian ⁠intelligence . Three Ukrainians were involved in sending two packages with GPS trackers and spare auto parts from Germany to Ukraine in an operation initiated by a Russian state entity, ⁠the court in Stuttgart said. The shipments were designed to identify opportunities for future sabotage. A 30-year-old was sentenced to one ⁠year and three months in prison for acting as an agent for the purposes of sabotage , but has already served his time in pre-trial custody. The two other defendants were acquitted ‌due to a lack of evidence that ‌they were knowingly involved in a plot to commit attacks. The three have been referred to as Vladyslav T, Daniil B and Yevhen B, with their full names withheld under German privacy rules. The Russian embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. European ‌governments have accused Moscow of a “hybrid war” against countries supporting Ukraine’s defence . In 2024, parcels shipped from Lithuania blew up in Germany, ​Poland and Britain. This month in ​Germany, officials found a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle airport. In the UK, a group of men were convicted in 2025 over an arson attack ordered by Russia’s terrorist Wagner group on a London warehouse linked to Ukraine. Several other cases have been before European courts. ‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last moments Read more Mikhail Fedorov, the sacked former defence minister of Ukraine, has called the country to hold elections , Dan Sabbagh writes . Fedorov said Ukraine had to “restore a full democratic process even amid a prolonged war”. Ukraine is in a state of martial law with elections forbidden by its constitution – however Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in 2025 that he was willing to hold elections if parliament permits it and international allies would assist. Donald Trump’s criticisms of Zelenskyy as “a dictator without elections” petered out after Zelenskyy challenged the US to help him hold them by organising a ceasefire with Russia, which has not eventuated. Estonia is investigating whether Russia was involved in an arson ⁠attack on a building housing a defence contractor , said the prime minister, Kristen Michal. The building used by Milrem Robotics, a maker of unmanned military weapons systems ⁠deployed in Ukraine and elsewhere, was targeted late on Friday. “The ⁠suspects have been identified. One of the lines of investigation ​is a possible ‌act of sabotage ‌and the involvement of Russia,” said Michal. The Russian embassy in Tallinn did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Ukrainian forces launched what appeared to be one of their biggest drone attacks on Russia since Moscow’s invasion over four years ago. Russia claimed at least 791 Ukrainian drones were launched into several regions, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the Black and the Azov seas. More than 600 Ukrainian drones flew towards Moscow, said the mayor, Sergei Sobyanin. Again, a Wildberries warehouse was hit, the company said, claiming the damage was insignificant. A Russian rocket attack killed 10 people in Pechenigya village in the Kharkiv region of north-east Ukraine . Another 18 were wounded, said Oleg Synegubov, the regional governor. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media that the strike hit a busy intersection, “a location with a post office and stores, surrounded only by residential buildings”. Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, said the UK would continue to stand by Ukraine after Russia levelled threats at London for supplying the Ukrainian military with drones that hit Russian soil . The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it had been informed that a drone exploded at a bus stop used by staff of the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant on Tuesday. Moscow-installed authorities at the illegally occupied Ukrainian-owned plant blamed Ukraine for a drone strike that killed a “nuclear specialist” and wounded 17 others. The IAEA said its chief, Rafael Grossi, called on military commanders to stop “unacceptable actions … [that pose] great risks to nuclear safety”. Both sides regularly accuse the other of carrying out strikes around the site, which Russia has militarised since seizing it in 2022. Meanwhile a ⁠power station in ⁠central Ukraine ⁠halted operations ​on Tuesday after ⁠it suffered significant damage from a ⁠Russian strike, ​power ‌firm ‌DTEK said. Ally Ross Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save The City of Hubbard has told Flock Safety that it will not be renewing its conract for Flock camera lincense plate readers, citing a need to cut costs. Cameras have already been taken down. Ally Ross has those details from Hubbard. The City of Hubbard has taken down its remaining Flock license plate readers after an unknown thief stole more than half of them, according to Police Chief Robert Thompson. Public records show that when the cameras were taken down in early August, the Hubbard City Police Department had already decided months earlier not to renew its contract with Flock Safety when it expires in November 2028. Thompson told 21 News his decision to end the partnership with Flock was motivated by cost-cutting. “Not that they weren't working, but the need for them wasn't as great as I thought it would be in our community,” Thomson said. “We did use them, but for the price tag, I think we could do something better.” Mayor Ben Kyle, through his administrative staff, declined to speak with 21 News about the Flock cameras. The staff member said only the police department, not the mayor’s office, was involved in the decision. When the city reached out to Flock in June, attempting to end their contract early, the company responded in an email stating that the city would still need to pay the remaining amount in its contract: $35,000. The city was given the option to keep the license plate readers in place until the contract expired, but after four out of the city’s six cameras were stolen a few weeks ago, the police department took the last two down. A Flock camera in Poland Township. August 27, 2026. “Had I left the other two up, I was afraid they were going to be stolen and cost us more money, and to replace those four that were stolen would also cost money,” Thompson said. “So if they were vandalized again or stolen again, it would cost us even more than what we wanted to spend.” The investigation into the thefts is ongoing, he said, and police have not yet recovered the technology. Hubbard is not the only local municipality ending its use of the cameras. Poland Township will also choose not to renew its contract with Flock next year, according to Police Chief Greg Wilson. The township only operates one camera, which faces the parking lot outside Poland Seminary High School. Wilson did not respond to 21 News’ request for more information on why the township is not renewing their contract. It comes as Flock cameras, and other automated license plate readers, have faced mounting scrutiny over privacy concerns. Thompson said his department heard a mix of feedback from citizens — some critical of the cameras, some supportive. “Our officers knew how to use it [and] knew how to use it properly,” Thompson said. “Any tool can be used or misused, so it all comes down to accountability and how it's managed.
